source_refs.note: Chapter 12 exercise (PDF 280-282, printed 277-279), solved: twelve MCQs with keys worked out from the chapter (no key is printed), fifteen short (Q15 in ten parts), twelve long and four inquisitive questions with model answers.

blocks.prompt: 1. Which structures are part of the appendicular skeleton?
blocks.explanation: The appendicular skeleton is the bones of the girdles and limbs; the humerus is the arm bone. The ethmoid (skull), ribs and lumbar vertebrae belong to the axial skeleton.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (c) is printed "Lumber vertebrae"; the correct term is lumbar vertebrae (the five vertebrae of the lower back).

blocks.prompt: 2. The term muscle fibre or myofibre refers to;
blocks.explanation: The individual cells of muscle are called muscle fibres or myofibres.

blocks.prompt: 3. Which of these extends the entire length of a muscle fibre?
blocks.explanation: Each muscle fibre contains 4 to 20 elongated thread-like myofibrils that run along its length; a sarcomere and the filaments are only short repeating units within a myofibril.

blocks.prompt: 4. Actin filaments are made of proteins;
blocks.explanation: Thin (actin) myofilaments are made of three proteins: a core of two twisted actin strands, two strands of tropomyosin wrapped around it, and troponin at regular intervals.

blocks.prompt: 5. In a muscle, the Z-line are the proteins for the attachment of the ends of;
blocks.explanation: The thin actin filaments are attached to protein discs called Z-lines; myosin filaments lie free in the middle of the sarcomere.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The stem is printed "the Z-line are the proteins"; singular and plural do not agree. It should read "the Z-lines are the proteins" (or "the Z-line is made of proteins").

blocks.prompt: 6. Sarcomere is a part between;
blocks.explanation: The section of a myofibril between two Z-lines is a sarcomere, the smallest unit of muscle contraction.

blocks.prompt: 7. Which part of muscle fibre releases calcium ions which trigger contraction?
blocks.explanation: The nerve impulse travels along the sarcolemma and T-tubules to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases calcium ions into the cytosol; calcium binds troponin and starts contraction.

blocks.prompt: 8. Which statement is correct to describe sliding filament model of muscle contraction?

options.text: Myosin filaments pull on the sarcomere so that actin filaments are shortened.
Myosin filaments pull on actin filaments so that sarcomere is shortened.
Actin filaments pull on myosin filaments so that sarcomere is shortened.
Actin filaments pull on sarcomere so that myosin filaments are shortened.

blocks.explanation: Myosin heads bind actin, form cross-bridges and bend towards the centre, pulling the actin filaments with them (power stroke); the sarcomere shortens while the filaments themselves do not shorten.

blocks.prompt: 9. When a muscle fibre shortens, which of the following also shortens?
blocks.explanation: In contraction the thin filaments slide past the thick ones; the Z-lines come closer, so each sarcomere shortens, while actin and myosin filaments keep their length.

blocks.prompt: 10. Which statement correctly describes an event of muscle contraction?

options.text: ATP binds to the actin binding site.
ATP is used to detach the myosin head from actin.

blocks.explanation: After the power stroke, a new ATP binds the myosin head, which lets the head detach from actin; splitting this ATP re-cocks the head. Myosin heads bind actin (not troponin), and it is tropomyosin that blocks the binding sites.

blocks.prompt: 11. Tendons connect bone and;
blocks.explanation: Tendons are tough connective tissues, formed at the ends of a skeletal muscle, that attach the muscle to bones; ligaments connect bone to bone.

blocks.prompt: 12. What is true about antagonistic pair of muscles?

options.text: It provides a backup if one of the muscles is injured
One muscle pushes while other pulls
It allows muscles to produce opposing movements
It doubles the strength of contraction

blocks.explanation: Muscles work in pairs that produce opposing actions: the flexor bends the joint and the extensor straightens it. Muscles can only pull, never push.

blocks.prompt: 1. Name three types of cells associated with bone and write their functions.
blocks.explanation:
1. Osteoblasts: bone-forming cells; they secrete the unmineralized ground substance (matrix).
2. Osteocytes: mature bone cells in lacunae; they maintain bone tissue and regulate the release of calcium from bone to blood.
3. Osteoclasts: develop from macrophages; they break down bone (resorption), releasing calcium and phosphate into blood, needed for growth and repair.

blocks.prompt: 2. Name the bones of cranium.
blocks.explanation:
Eight cranial bones:
Paired: 2 parietal and 2 temporal bones.
Unpaired: frontal, occipital, ethmoid and sphenoid bones.

blocks.prompt: 3. Enlist the bones in the five groups of vertebrae.
blocks.explanation:
33 vertebrae:
1. Cervical: 7 (neck; 1st atlas, 2nd axis).
2. Thoracic: 12 (chest; carry ribs).
3. Lumbar: 5 (abdominal region).
4. Sacral: 5 (fused into the sacrum).
5. Coccygeal: 4 (fused into the coccyx).

blocks.prompt: 4. What bones make the rib cage?
blocks.explanation:
12 pairs (24) of ribs and the sternum (chest bone), with the ribs joined at the back to the 12 thoracic vertebrae.
Ribs 1-7 (true) join the sternum by their own costal cartilages, 8-10 (false) by a common cartilage, and 11-12 (floating) do not reach it.

blocks.prompt: 5. Name the bones of pectoral girdle and pelvic girdle.
blocks.explanation:
Pectoral girdle: a pair of clavicles (collar bones) and a pair of scapulae (shoulder bones).
Pelvic girdle: two hip bones; each is made of three fused bones, the ilium (printed "ileum"), ischium and pubis, which form the acetabulum. The hip bones meet in front at the pubic symphysis.

blocks.prompt: 6. Name the bones of forelimbs and hindlimbs.
blocks.explanation:
Forelimb (30 bones): 1 humerus, 1 radius, 1 ulna, 8 carpals (printed "carpels"), 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges.
Hindlimb (30 bones): 1 femur, 1 patella, 1 tibia, 1 fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges.

blocks.prompt: 7. What is fibrous joint? Give examples.
blocks.explanation:
A fibrous (immovable) joint is one in which the bones are directly joined by fibrous connective tissue, mainly collagen, so no movement is possible.
Examples: sutures between skull bones; joint between tibia and fibula; joints of teeth with their sockets in the jawbone.

blocks.prompt: 8. Name the steps involved in bone repair.
blocks.explanation:
(Beyond the chapter; the chapter only says osteoclasts and osteoblasts work in repair.)
1. Haematoma (blood clot) forms at the break.
2. Soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus forms, joining the broken ends.
3. Hard (bony) callus: osteoblasts replace the cartilage with new bone.
4. Remodelling: osteoclasts remove extra bone and the bone regains its shape.

blocks.prompt: 9. What skeletal structures are affected from the osteoarthritis?
blocks.explanation:
Osteoarthritis affects the articular cartilage at the ends of bones in joints, which gradually softens and disintegrates.
Mainly affected: knee joints, hip joints and intervertebral joints.

blocks.prompt: 10. List the major parts of skeletal muscle fibre.
blocks.explanation:
1. Sarcolemma (plasma membrane) and its T-tubules.
2. Sarcoplasm (cytoplasm) with many nuclei.
3. Sarcoplasmic reticulum (stores and releases Ca²⁺).
4. Myofibrils (4-20), made of thick myosin and thin actin filaments arranged in sarcomeres (Z-lines, A-band, I-band, H-zone).

blocks.prompt: 11. What do you mean by I-band, A-band and H-zone?
blocks.explanation:
I-band: light band of thin (actin) filaments only, on either side of a Z-line.
A-band: dark band; the whole length of the thick (myosin) filaments, including where actin overlaps them.
H-zone: the lighter central region of the A-band where only myosin is present (no overlap); it narrows or disappears in contraction.

blocks.prompt: 12. Describe the antagonistic arrangement of skeletal muscles.
blocks.explanation:
To move a bone at a joint in two directions, muscles work in pairs that produce opposing actions (antagonistic arrangement). The flexor contracts to bend the joint while the extensor relaxes; the extensor contracts to straighten it while the flexor relaxes.
Example: at the knee, hamstrings (flexor) and quadriceps (extensor).

blocks.prompt: 13. Ligaments are elastic while tendons are hard. Justify.
blocks.explanation:
Ligaments join bone to bone at joints; they contain elastic fibres and stretch a little, so the joint can move while its bones stay held together.
Tendons join muscle to bone; they are made of dense, tough collagen that hardly stretches, so the full pull of the muscle reaches the bone. (Partly beyond the chapter.)

blocks.prompt: 14. Draw a diagram of sarcomere and label its parts.
blocks.explanation:
How to draw (a horizontal sarcomere):
1. Draw two vertical lines at the ends: the Z-lines. The part between them is one sarcomere.
2. From each Z-line draw thin horizontal lines towards the centre: actin (thin) filaments.
3. In the middle draw thicker lines that overlap the inner ends of the actin: myosin (thick) filaments, with small heads (cross-bridges) towards the actin.
4. Draw a vertical line at the centre through the myosin: the M-line.
Labels: Z-line, sarcomere (Z to Z), actin filament, myosin filament, A-band (whole myosin length), I-band (actin only, by the Z-lines), H-zone (centre, myosin only), M-line.

blocks.prompt: 1. Explain the structure of bone.
blocks.explanation:
Bone is connective tissue reinforced with calcium and specialized bone cells. It is a moist, living tissue.
1. Periosteum: a tough membrane covering the bone's surface; collagen fibres anchor it to the bone beneath.
2. Compact bone: the thick, hard layer under the periosteum; it makes up most of the bone tissue. Its structural units are Haversian systems, each made of:
   - Lamellae: concentric layers of mineralized matrix containing collagen fibres (flexible) and needle-shaped calcium phosphate crystals (rigid), so bone is both strong and flexible.
   - Lacunae and osteocytes: small spaces between lamellae holding mature bone cells (osteocytes), linked to each other and to the Haversian canal by canaliculi.
   - Haversian canal: the central canal containing blood vessels, nerves and lymphatic vessels.
   - Perpendicular channels connect the Haversian canals with each other and with the periosteum.
3. Spongy bone: beneath compact bone; a latticework of bony spikes, light and strong.
4. Bone marrow: red marrow (in spongy bone, ends of long bones, ribs, vertebrae, sternum, pelvis) makes RBCs, WBCs and platelets; yellow marrow (in the shaft of long bones) is mostly fat, an energy reserve, and can turn red after severe blood loss.
5. Bone cells: osteoblasts (form bone), osteocytes (maintain bone, regulate calcium), osteoclasts (resorb bone).
6. Parts of a long bone: broad ends are the epiphyses; the shaft is the diaphysis.

blocks.prompt: 2. Describe the structure of three types of cartilage.
blocks.explanation:
General structure of cartilage:
1. Perichondrium: a layer of connective tissue around the cartilage, with blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves that supply it.
2. Matrix: made of collagen, elastin, proteoglycans and other fibres; it gives strength, flexibility and resistance to compression. It has no blood vessels, so cells are supplied by diffusion and cartilage heals slowly.
3. Chondrocytes: cartilage cells in small spaces (lacunae) in the matrix; they make and maintain the matrix.
Three types:
1. Hyaline cartilage: the most common type; a smooth, glassy matrix with fine collagen fibres (fibre detail beyond the chapter). Found in the nose, trachea and on the articulating surfaces of bones in joints (articular cartilage).
2. Fibrocartilage: matrix with thick bundles of collagen fibres (beyond the chapter), so it is the toughest; found where there is high stress and tension: intervertebral discs and pubic symphysis.
3. Elastic cartilage: matrix with many elastic fibres (beyond the chapter), so it is flexible and springs back; found in the external ear and epiglottis.

blocks.prompt: 3. Write the cause and symptoms of joint dislocation, spondylosis, and sciatica.
blocks.explanation:
Joint dislocation (bones of a joint forced out of their normal positions):
Causes: a sudden impact or trauma; rheumatoid arthritis can also cause it. A severe dislocation can tear muscles, ligaments and tendons.
Symptoms: swelling, intense pain and immobility of the joint.
(Correction to the book: it is put back by a doctor, not a physiotherapist; surgery may be needed to tighten stretched ligaments.)
Spondylosis (degeneration of vertebrae, intervertebral discs, ligaments or cartilage of the vertebral column):
Causes: natural degeneration of intervertebral discs with ageing (most common), genetic factors, trauma, prolonged poor posture and obesity. Discs narrow and fuse and bony outgrowths form, pressing on nerves or the spinal cord; most common in the neck (cervical) and lower back (lumbar).
Symptoms: back or neck pain, stiffness and reduced range of motion.
Sciatica (compression or irritation of the sciatic nerve, which runs from the lower back through the buttocks into each leg):
Causes: often a herniated (slipped) or bulging disc pressing on the nerve; also trauma, infection, inflammation and spondylosis.
Symptoms: pain or discomfort in the lower back, buttocks, legs or feet; tingling or numbness in the legs or feet; weakness or difficulty in moving the legs or feet.

blocks.prompt: 4. Describe the types of arthritis, with their causes, symptoms and treatments.
blocks.explanation:
Arthritis includes different inflammatory conditions of the joints. Symptoms common to all: joint pain and stiffness, with redness, warmth and swelling of the joints.
1. Osteoarthritis (the most common type):
Cause: the articular cartilage at the ends of bones in joints gradually softens and disintegrates (wear with age).
Joints: knee, hip and intervertebral joints.
2. Rheumatoid arthritis:
Cause: an autoimmune disorder in which the synovial membrane becomes inflamed.
Joints: most commonly the wrists and hands; it can also cause dislocation.
3. Gouty arthritis (gout):
Cause: build-up of uric acid in the blood, which forms crystals in the joints and causes inflammation.
Joints: most commonly the big toe; also knees, wrists and fingers.
Treatment (beyond the chapter; the chapter gives no treatment for arthritis):
- Pain-relieving and anti-inflammatory medicines; rest, warm or cold packs and physiotherapy.
- Weight control and gentle exercise (osteoarthritis); immune-suppressing drugs (rheumatoid arthritis); less red meat, plenty of water and uric-acid-lowering drugs (gout).
- Joint replacement (total or partial) or chondrocyte implantation for badly damaged joints (described in the chapter's joint transplantation box).

blocks.prompt: 5. Describe the three types of muscles.
blocks.explanation:
Muscle is tissue that contracts in a coordinated way to move body parts or the whole body. Human body has three types:
1. Skeletal muscle:
- Location/function: attached to bones by tendons; moves limbs, trunk and face (moves the skeleton).
- Fibres: long, cylindrical, multinucleated cells with regular striations.
- Control: voluntary (consciously controlled).
2. Smooth muscle:
- Location/function: walls of the stomach, intestines, blood vessels and other internal organs; moves substances through hollow organs.
- Fibres: spindle-shaped, single nucleus, no striations, surrounded by connective tissue.
- Control: involuntary.
3. Cardiac muscle:
- Location/function: only in the walls of the heart; pumps blood.
- Fibres: branched, striated (irregular stripes), usually one central nucleus per cell.
- Control: involuntary.

blocks.prompt: 6. Explain the ultrastructure of skeletal muscle.
blocks.explanation:
Organization: a skeletal muscle is made of bundles of muscle fibres (cells) enclosed by collagen and connective tissue, which forms tendons at the ends. Each fibre contains myofibrils; each myofibril is made of myofilaments (myosin and actin).
Muscle fibre:
1. A long, cylindrical, multinucleated cell enclosed by the sarcolemma (plasma membrane).
2. Its cytoplasm is the sarcoplasm, containing the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), which stores Ca²⁺.
3. The sarcolemma dips deep into the cell as transverse (T) tubules that reach the ends of the SR.
4. It contains 4-20 thread-like myofibrils.
Myofibril and sarcomere:
1. Thick filaments of myosin form dark A-bands; thin filaments of actin form light I-bands; this alternation gives striations.
2. Thin filaments are attached to protein discs, the Z-lines. The part between two Z-lines is a sarcomere, the smallest unit of contraction.
3. Within a sarcomere, actin extends from each Z-line towards the centre and overlaps myosin; the lighter centre of the A-band with no overlap is the H-band (zone); a dark M-line at its centre stabilizes the thick filaments.
Myofilaments:
1. Thick filament (about 16 nm): many myosin molecules, each of two intertwined polypeptide chains ending in a globular head that binds actin (cross-bridges).
2. Thin filament (7-8 nm): two twisted actin strands; two tropomyosin strands that stiffen it and block the myosin-binding sites at rest; troponin (three polypeptides: binding actin, tropomyosin and calcium).

blocks.prompt: 7. Write a detailed note on the sliding filament model of muscle contraction.
blocks.explanation:
According to the sliding filament model, a muscle contracts when its thin (actin) filaments slide past the thick (myosin) filaments so that they overlap more; the filaments themselves do not shorten.
1. Relaxed sarcomere: sarcomeres are at normal length. Myosin heads cannot bind actin because tropomyosin blocks the binding sites; troponin is attached to tropomyosin. Each myosin head has already split ATP into ADP and Pi (it is "cocked").
2. Arrival of the nerve impulse: the motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the synapse; the impulse travels along the sarcolemma and T-tubules to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases Ca²⁺ into the cytosol. Ca²⁺ binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin away from the binding sites on actin.
3. Cross-bridges and power stroke: myosin heads bind the exposed sites, forming cross-bridges. They release ADP and Pi, change shape and bend towards the centre of the sarcomere, pulling the actin filaments with them (power stroke). Z-lines come closer, the sarcomere shortens, I-band narrows and the H-zone disappears, while the A-bands keep their length but come closer. This happens in all sarcomeres at once, so the whole muscle contracts.
4. Detachment: a new ATP binds each myosin head, letting it detach from actin. Splitting this ATP into ADP and Pi re-cocks the head, and the cycle repeats as long as Ca²⁺ and ATP are present.
Relaxation (beyond the chapter's steps): when impulses stop, Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the SR, tropomyosin covers the sites again and the muscle relaxes.
Note: after death no ATP is made, so cross-bridges cannot detach: rigor mortis.

blocks.prompt: 8. Explain the action of antagonistic muscles in the movement of knee joint.
blocks.explanation:
Muscles can only pull, so to move a joint in two directions they work in antagonistic pairs: when one (flexor) contracts the other (extensor) relaxes, and vice versa. Each muscle has an origin on the stationary bone and an insertion on the bone that moves.
The knee joint lies between the femur (thigh bone) and the tibia and fibula (lower leg bones). It is a hinge joint.
1. Flexion (bending) of the lower leg: done by the hamstrings, a group of three muscles at the back of the thigh. Origin: pelvic girdle and top of the femur. Insertion: upper parts of the tibia and fibula. When the hamstrings contract, the lower leg bends and the quadriceps relax.
2. Extension (straightening) of the lower leg: done by the quadriceps, a group of four muscles at the front of the thigh. Origin: ilium (pelvic girdle) and femur. Insertion: patella (kneecap) and tibia. When the quadriceps contract, the lower leg straightens and the hamstrings relax.
So the hamstrings are the flexor and the quadriceps the extensor of the knee; their alternate contraction and relaxation allow walking, running and kicking.

blocks.prompt: 9. Draw a diagram of sarcomere and label its parts.
blocks.explanation:
Labelled diagram of a sarcomere (draw it horizontally), step by step:
1. Draw two vertical lines at the left and right ends and label each "Z-line". Mark the distance between them with a double arrow: "Sarcomere".
2. From each Z-line draw several thin parallel horizontal lines running towards the centre, stopping short of the middle: label "Actin (thin filament)".
3. In the middle draw thicker parallel lines lying between the actin lines and overlapping their inner ends; draw small projections from them towards actin: label "Myosin (thick filament)" and "Cross-bridges (myosin heads)".
4. Draw a vertical line at the exact centre through the myosin: label "M-line".
5. Mark the bands with brackets:
   - "A-band" (dark): the full length of the myosin filaments.
   - "H-zone": the central part of the A-band where there is myosin only (no actin).
   - "I-band" (light): the region of actin only on each side of a Z-line (half an I-band at each end of the sarcomere).
6. (Optional) Draw a second, contracted sarcomere below it: Z-lines closer, I-band and H-zone narrower, A-band the same length.
Labels to show: Z-line, sarcomere, actin filament, myosin filament, cross-bridges, M-line, A-band, I-band, H-zone.

blocks.prompt: 10. Describe causes and symptoms of muscle fatigue, cramps and tetany.
blocks.explanation:
Muscle fatigue (decline in muscle performance after prolonged or intense activity or due to disease):
Causes:
1. ATP supply is depleted, so the muscle can no longer contract.
2. Metabolic wastes build up (lactate, hydrogen ions, reactive oxygen).
3. Repeatedly activated fibres cannot handle calcium ions effectively.
4. Small damage to fibres from intense exercise causes inflammation.
Symptoms: pain, decreased muscle strength and reduced endurance. It improves with rest; severe cases need medical attention.
Muscle cramps (sudden, involuntary, often painful contractions lasting seconds to minutes, mostly in legs and feet):
Causes: dehydration, imbalance of salts, overuse or injury of the muscle, certain medicines (e.g. diuretics), and diseases such as diabetes, liver disease and nerve damage.
Symptoms: sudden painful tightening of the muscle. Relief: gentle stretching and massage, heat or cold, pain-relieving medicines.
Tetany (involuntary contractions or spasms due to increased muscle tone and hyperexcitable nerves):
Causes: most commonly hypocalcaemia (low blood calcium) due to vitamin D deficiency, renal failure or thyroid disorders; also other salt imbalances such as low magnesium.
Symptoms: spasms in the hands, feet, face or larynx. Treatment depends on the cause: calcium or magnesium supplements or intravenous fluids.

blocks.prompt: 11. Justify how the main functions of the skeleton are to act as a system of rods and levers.
blocks.explanation:
1. Rods: bones are rigid rods (strong yet flexible because of calcium phosphate crystals and collagen) that give the body structure and support and protect internal organs.
2. Fulcrum: joints act as the fulcrums (pivot points) about which the bones turn, allowing movement.
3. Effort: skeletal muscles attached to bones by tendons pull on them and provide the effort (force).
4. Load: the weight or resistance moved (body part or object) is the load.
Example: lifting a weight in the hand: the forearm bones (radius and ulna) are the lever, the elbow joint is the fulcrum, the biceps provides the effort and the weight is the load. (The book says the biceps acts as the lever; correctly the forearm is the lever and the biceps gives the effort.)
Because muscles only pull, antagonistic pairs (biceps/triceps, hamstrings/quadriceps) work each lever in both directions. Thus support, protection and movement all come from the skeleton working as rods and levers.

blocks.prompt: 12. Justify why do the muscles pull but do not push.
blocks.explanation:
1. Muscle fibres can do only one active thing: contract and shorten. When the myosin heads pull the actin filaments, sarcomeres shorten; there is no mechanism by which they actively lengthen.
2. A muscle is attached by tendons to two bones (origin on the fixed bone, insertion on the moving bone). On contraction it pulls the insertion towards the origin and the bone moves.
3. When the muscle relaxes it cannot push the bone back; it becomes soft and is stretched back to its length by the pull of the opposing (antagonistic) muscle, or by gravity.
4. That is why muscles are arranged in antagonistic pairs: e.g. at the knee the hamstrings pull to bend it and the quadriceps pull to straighten it.
(The book's box says muscles are usually attached to bone at only one end; in fact skeletal muscles are attached at both ends, as the book itself says under origin and insertion. The real reason is that fibres can only actively shorten.)

blocks.prompt: 1. Why is calcium essential for both the structural integrity of bones and the process of muscle contraction?
blocks.explanation:
Bones: the matrix of the lamellae contains needle-shaped calcium phosphate crystals, which make bone rigid and strong; with collagen it is strong and flexible. Lack of calcium (and of vitamin D, which helps absorb it) weakens bones (osteoporosis).
Muscle: Ca²⁺ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin; only then can cross-bridges form and the muscle contract. Low blood calcium (hypocalcaemia) causes tetany.
Link: bone is also the body's calcium store; osteocytes and osteoclasts release calcium into blood when needed, keeping a steady supply for muscles and nerves.

blocks.prompt: 2. Why is the human skeleton designed with both rigid bones and flexible joints instead of being made of a single solid structure?
blocks.explanation:
1. Rigid bones give support, shape and protection (skull for brain, rib cage for heart and lungs) and act as levers.
2. Joints between them act as fulcrums, so muscles can move parts in many directions: ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (elbow, knee), pivot, saddle, gliding joints. A single solid structure could not move.
3. Cartilage at joints and intervertebral discs absorb shock and reduce friction, protecting bones and brain from jolts.
4. Small separate bones allow growth at their ends and repair of one part without affecting the whole; flexible joints also allow breathing (rib movement) and an upright bipedal posture with balance (S-curved vertebral column, arched foot).

blocks.prompt: 3. Why do muscles always work in pairs (antagonistic muscles) rather than alone?
blocks.explanation:
1. A muscle can only pull (contract); it cannot push itself back to its original length.
2. So one muscle can move a bone in only one direction. To bring it back, a second muscle on the opposite side must pull it the other way.
3. In each pair, when the flexor contracts (bends the joint) the extensor relaxes, and when the extensor contracts (straightens it) the flexor relaxes: e.g. biceps and triceps at the elbow, hamstrings and quadriceps at the knee.
4. Working in pairs also gives smooth, controlled movement and holds the joint steady (posture).

blocks.prompt: 4. Why does prolonged inactivity or space travel lead to muscle atrophy and bone weakening??
blocks.explanation:
(Beyond the chapter, built on it.)
1. Bones and muscles are living tissues that adapt to the load placed on them. Lack of weight-bearing exercise weakens bones (the chapter lists it as a cause of osteoporosis).
2. In bed rest or in the weightlessness of space, bones bear no body weight and muscles work against no gravity. Osteoclasts then break down bone faster than osteoblasts build it; calcium is lost into the blood and urine, so bone density falls.
3. Unused muscle fibres lose their proteins (actin and myosin) and become thinner and weaker: muscle atrophy, especially in leg and back muscles that normally support posture.
4. Prevention: regular exercise, e.g. astronauts use treadmills and resistance machines in space; patients do physiotherapy.
